annotations.text:
THE DESIGN SYSTEM

Taken from the Fuse wallet screens and applied to the whole product. Six rules carry it.

1. The page is white. Grey only ever appears as a card, never behind one.
2. Titles are true black and heavy. Everything supporting them is a light grey.
3. Money splits in two. The whole number is black and heavy, the decimal is two thirds the size and pale.
4. An icon is a rounded square in its own saturated colour with a white glyph.
5. A card is either a flat grey fill or a dashed outline. Nothing casts a shadow except a button, the ask bar and a sheet.
6. A sheet rises over a page that is dimmed and blurred, and floats clear of all four edges.

THE SCALES

Six type sizes and nothing between them. 12, 14, 16, 22, 26 and 36. The whole ramp came down a step after a pass over the home screen, so the product reads quieter than the reference does.

Money never uses 12. Below about twelve and a half pixels the Naira sign loses its crossbars, so any figure is lifted to 14.

Three weights. Regular for anything grey, bold for anything named, heavy for money.

A four point spacing rhythm plus 56 and 72, which are structural. A page starts 72 from the top, which clears the status bar. Seven corner radii and one pill.

All of it is enforced when the files are generated, so nothing can drift.

CONTRAST, AND WHAT IT COST

Two decisions compound here. The reference greys were matched exactly, and then the whole type ramp came down a step. Light grey and small text together.

Measured across all eighteen screens, 553 pieces of text: 367 pass, 186 do not. Every failure is one of the three greys or the pale kobo.

Nothing that carries meaning on its own fails. Titles, figures, amounts, row names and buttons are black on white. What fails is the second line under a title, which repeats what the icon and the title already say.

Green and red text and the small blue captions were darkened, because the reference has no green or red text to copy.

THE BAR AT THE BOTTOM

The reference puts three tab icons on the left and a black circle on the right, with no bar behind them.

This product replaces the tabs with the model. The cog stays, then the ask bar takes the width, then the black circle keeps its corner.

On every screen except home, the cog is replaced by back, so back lives at the bottom left where the reference puts it.

The black circle opens send, receive, activity and bills over a blurred page. That is the only place those four live, so no screen has to carry them.

1. Home

The whole top block is deliberately small. A kicker, the balance, one button. The balance at sixty pixels was eating the fold and pushing the model's first card off the screen, so it came down to thirty six with the kobo at twenty two.

The four services are one flat row rather than a grid of tiles, which saves about a hundred and ninety pixels. Colour still does the finding.

Everything under Activities is the feed. The model's most useful card leads it, because on a screen this size the first thing you read decides what the app is.

2. The black circle

Send money, receive, activity and pay a bill. Four things you do most, over the page blurred and dimmed.

They stagger up from the circle and the circle turns into a cross. Tapping the cross, the blur, or pressing escape puts them away.

This is where money movement lives. It keeps the grid free for services and the ask bar free for the model.

3. Add money

The reference's sheet, with our content. A big coloured icon, a title, a grey line under it, a cross in the corner and three rows.

The sheet floats ten pixels clear of every edge rather than sitting on the bottom. That is what makes it read as a sheet and not a screen.

4. Asking

You hold the ask bar and talk. The words appear as you say them, and the part the model is still deciding on stays grey.

It uses the same blur as the other two overlays, so all three feel like one behaviour rather than three.

Nothing here is a chat log. Speech turns into a screen.

5. An answer

A question about money gets a screen, not a paragraph. The figure, the trend, the chart and the breakdown.

The chips under the chart show what the model understood. Tap one and you change the question rather than typing it again.

The line at the bottom says where the number came from, so you can check it.

6. Sending money

The model prepares, you confirm. Every part it filled in sits in a pale blue panel with a line saying where it got it.

So you check three small things instead of typing four fields. Blue means the model wrote it. Black means you have to press it.

7. Done

A green tick, the amount, the receipt, then one offer to make it automatic.

The offer only appears after something worked. That is the moment it is worth asking.

Taking a loan ends here too, and it gets no tick and no cheer.

9. Settings

This is the reference screen copied most closely, because it is the clearest statement of their list style.

A bordered promotion row with a filled black chevron, then grey group headings, then rows with coloured icons and pale chevrons. Nothing between the rows.

10. All services

Forty things without an icon wall. The eight you use are a grid, everything else is a list under a plain heading.

There is no search bar on the page any more. The ask bar at the bottom is the search bar, on every screen.

11. Buying data

You said four words. The model filled in who, what and how much, and each one says where it came from.

The money you get back goes to your savings goal instead of coming back as cash. Same money, better place.

12. Before you pay

The same prepared card, for electricity. The meter you always use, and about what you spent last month.

Three amounts underneath with what they buy in units, because nobody thinks in Naira for electricity.

13. After you pay

The token is the point of this screen, so it is the biggest thing on it with a copy button under it.

Then the receipt, then one offer to make it monthly.

14. Bills

Everything that repeats, and which of them are covered. The bar is segments, not a percentage, because a percentage is a number you can farm.

Paid bills go grey and stay in place, so the list is the whole month rather than only what is left.

15. Borrowing

The whole cost before you decide. What you get, the interest, the fee, what you pay back and when.

The late fee and the credit bureau are on the screen, not in terms and conditions.

There is no progress bar towards a bigger limit. That is the one mechanic that would reliably lift borrowing, and it is left out on purpose.

16. Virtual card

A card made for one merchant, with its own limit. Reveal, freeze, fund and rules, each in its own colour.

The limit bar is the real control here. When it fills, the card stops working, which is the whole reason to make one.

17. A goal

The one piece of gamification in the product, and it is progress towards something you chose.

The research is clear that points and badges move engagement and not behaviour, and that visible progress towards your own goal is what holds up.

So the ring is the only score, and it counts money you actually put aside. Nothing is locked.

18. Standing instructions

What the model may do without asking. Three switches, each with a log of what it has already done.

Under them, in plain words, the three things it will always ask about first. That list is what makes the switches above it safe to turn on.

8. History

The reference list style, with amounts. No dividers, no card, just height and colour doing the separating.

Money coming in is green with a plus, money going out is black with a minus. All, In and Out at the top really switch.

It is called History and not Activity because the home screen already has a heading called Activities, and those are two different things.
